final_message:
All three versions are written and give the correct output on s1, s2 and s3. They also matched a simple reference script on 76 random edge-case inputs, and agreed with each other on an 89 MB generated file of 10M words.

The machine was at 90–100% CPU from other programs the whole time, so my timings are rough. On the 89 MB file: Rust about 0.4–1.3 s, `fast.py` about 6 s, `plain.py` about 12–18 s.

**Algorithm (all versions):** split the text into words, folding to lower case. Find where sentences end (`.`, `!`, `?`), count each pair of adjacent words in the same sentence, and print the top 20, breaking ties by first word then second word.

**Rust (`rust/src/main.rs`)**
- **Finding words:** SSE2 instructions build 64-bit masks of letters and sentence ends for each 64-byte block, so there is no per-byte branching. Word starts are found by bit tricks on those masks.
- **Word lookup:** a word of up to 16 letters is read in a single 16-byte load, and its length is worked out without a loop. That packed value is the key to a hash table I wrote, which stays in cache at this vocabulary size. Longer words go to a standard `HashMap`.
- **Pair counting:** words are numbered in alphabetical order, so sorting the pair keys also gives the tie-break order. A pair key fits in 32 bits when the vocabulary is under 65,536 words; otherwise it uses 64 bits. The keys are sorted with a radix sort and counted run by run in one pass.
- **Build settings:** in `[profile.release]` I set `lto = "fat"`, `codegen-units = 1` and `panic = "abort"`. It uses one thread and no rayon.

**`plain.py`**
- One `bytes.translate` lower-cases letters, turns `!` and `?` into `.`, and turns every other character into a space. Then `replace(b".", b" . ")` and `str.split()` do the tokenizing in C, which was about 3× faster than `re.findall`.
- Pairs are counted with `Counter.update`. Pairs touching a sentence end are filtered out before counting, also in C (`itertools.compress` with `operator.ne`), which cut counting time by about 30%.
- The text is processed in 4 MB chunks so the token lists stay small.
- The 20th-highest count is found with `heapq.nlargest`, then only pairs at or above it are sorted.

**`fast.py` (NumPy)**
- **Finding words:** all vectorized: a letter mask, word edges with `flatnonzero`, and the 12-letter key of each word built by packing each letter into 5 bits in place. Words longer than 12 letters get their ids in further vectorized rounds of 12 letters; only words over 48 letters use a Python dict.
- **Word ids:** on this machine `np.argsort` was very slow (about 4 s for 10M keys) while `np.sort` took 0.3 s. So I sort only to get the distinct words, then map every word to its id with a hash table looked up in bulk.
- **Pair counting:** sentence breaks come from `logical_or.reduceat`. Pair counts come from `np.sort` and run lengths, and the top 20 come from `np.partition`.
- **Bug found and fixed:** the random tests caught a tie-break error when two different first words share their first 12 letters. It is fixed.

**Passing samples:** s1, s2 and s3 pass in all three versions.

The test helpers are in `bench/`: `gen.py` makes benchmark-style input, `ref.py` is the slow reference, and `edge.py` makes random edge cases. I deleted the large generated files.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
